readings.c1s3:
¶
{{smaller block|Our last horses were so slow that the postilion, a handsome, lively boy, whose pride was a little ''touched'' by my remonstrances, failed, in spite of all his efforts, to bring us to the station before seven.
{{right|''B. Taylor'', Northern Travel, p. 43.}}}}

'''21.''' To fall upon; strike; affect; impress.

{{smaller block|If . . . any air of music ''touch'' their ears,
You shall perceive them make a mutual stand.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., v. 1. 76.}}
What of sweet before
Hath ''touch'd'' my sense flat seems to this.
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ix. 987.}}}}

'''22.''' To affect or move mentally or emotionally; fill with passion or tender feeling; affect or move, as with pity; hence, to melt; soften.

{{smaller block|He is ''touch'd''
To the noble heart. ''Shak.'', W. T., iii. 2. 222.
He weeps again;
His heart is ''touch'd'', sure, with remorse.
{{right|''Fletcher'', Wife for a Month, iv. 1.}}
Tremendous scene! that gen'ral horror gave,
But ''touch'd'' with joy the bosoms of the brave.
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xiii. 435.}}}}

'''23.''' To make an impression on; have an effect on; act on.

{{smaller block|Its face must be . . . so hard that a file will not ''touch'' it.
{{right|''J. Moxon'', Mech. Exercises.}}}}

'''24.''' To influence by impulse; impel forcibly.

{{smaller block|No decree of mine
Concurring to necessitate his fall,
Or ''touch'' with lightest moment of impulse
His free will. ''Milton'', P. L., x. 45.}}

'''25.''' To affect; concern; relate to.

{{smaller block|With that the quene was wroth in hir maner,
Thought she anon this ''towchith'' me right ner.
{{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 560.}}}}

{{RunningHeader|touch|6401|touch}}'''12.''' Of a musical instrument, to cause to sound; play: usually applied to instruments that are sounded by striking or twanging, but extended to others. {{smaller block|''Touch'' thy instrument a strain or two. {{right|''Shak.'', J. C., iv. 3. 257.}}}} {{smaller block|I'll ''touch'' my horn. {{right|''Massinger'', Guardian, ii. 4.}}}} '''13.''' To perform on an instrument, as a piece of music. {{smaller block|A person in the royal retinue ''touched'' a light and lively air on the flageolet. {{right|''Scott.''}}}} '''14.''' To paint or form by touches or strokes as of a pen or brush; mark or delineate by light touches or strokes, as an artist. {{smaller block|Such heavenly touches ne'er ''touch'd'' earthly faces. {{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, xvii.}}}} {{smaller block|The lines, though ''touch'd'' but faintly, are drawn right. {{right|''Pope'', Essay on Criticism, l. 22.}}}} '''15.''' To improve or finish, as a drawing, by adding a stroke here and there, as with a pen, pencil, or brush; retouch: usually with ''up''. {{smaller block|What he saw was only her natural countenance, ''touched up'' with the usual improvements of an aged Coquette. {{right|''Addison'', Freeholder, No. 44.}}}} {{smaller block|My impression [of an engraving] is unequal, being faint in some parts, very dark in others. If the plate was worn, it has been ''touched'' afterwards. {{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., X. 118.}}}} '''16.''' To take, as food, drink, etc.; help one's self to; hence, to partake of; taste. {{smaller block|If thou sytte be a worthyor man Then thy self, . . . Suffre hym fyrste to ''towche'' the mete Ere thy self any ther-of gete. {{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 14.}}}} {{smaller block|He dies that ''touches'' any of this fruit Till I and my affairs are answered. {{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, ii. 7. 98.}}}} '''17.''' To infect or impair by contact; stain; blot; blemish; taint. {{smaller block|The life of all his blood Is ''touch'd'' corruptibly. ''Shak.'', K. John, v. 7. 2.}} {{smaller block|Thou canst not ''touch'' my credit; Truth will not suffer me to be abus'd thus. {{right|''Fletcher'' (''and Massinger''?), Lovers' Progress, iii. 6.}}}} '''18.''' To impair mentally in some slight degree; affect slightly with craziness: used chiefly in the past participle. {{smaller block|Madam, you see master's a little—''touched'', that's all. Twenty ounces of blood let loose would set all right again. {{right|''Vanbrugh'', Confederacy, v. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|Pray mind him not, his brain is ''touch'd''. {{right|''Steele'', Lying Lover, v. 1.}}}} '''19†.''' To attack; hence, to animadvert upon; take to task; censure; reprove; ridicule. {{smaller block|Sur Water Hungerfo and his brother hathe ''touched'' me in iij thinges, but I wolde in no case have ye douches to knowe them for geving hur grefe. {{right|''Darrell Papers'' (1570) (H. Hall, Society in Elizabethan Age, App., ii.).}}}} {{smaller block|You teach behaviours! Or ''touch'' us for our freedoms! {{right|''Fletcher'', Wildgoose Chase, ii. 3.}}}} '''20.''' To sting; nettle, as with some sharp speech. {{smaller block|Beshrew me, but his words have ''touch'd'' me home. {{right|''Ford'', Perkin Warbeck, ii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|Our last horses were so slow that the postilion, a handsome, lively boy, whose pride was a little ''touched'' by my remonstrances, failed, in spite of all his efforts, to bring us to the station before seven. {{right|''B. Taylor'', Northern Travel, p. 43.}}}} '''21.''' To fall upon; strike; affect; impress. {{smaller block|If . . . any air of music ''touch'' their ears, You shall perceive them make a mutual stand. {{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., v. 1. 76.}} What of sweet before Hath ''touch'd'' my sense flat seems to this. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., ix. 987.}}}} '''22.''' To affect or move mentally or emotionally; fill with passion or tender feeling; affect or move, as with pity; hence, to melt; soften. {{smaller block|He is ''touch'd'' To the noble heart. ''Shak.'', W. T., iii. 2. 222. He weeps again; His heart is ''touch'd'', sure, with remorse. {{right|''Fletcher'', Wife for a Month, iv. 1.}} Tremendous scene! that gen'ral horror gave, But ''touch'd'' with joy the bosoms of the brave. {{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xiii. 435.}}}} '''23.''' To make an impression on; have an effect on; act on. {{smaller block|Its face must be . . . so hard that a file will not ''touch'' it. {{right|''J. Moxon'', Mech. Exercises.}}}} '''24.''' To influence by impulse; impel forcibly. {{smaller block|No decree of mine Concurring to necessitate his fall, Or ''touch'' with lightest moment of impulse His free will. ''Milton'', P. L., x. 45.}} '''25.''' To affect; concern; relate to. {{smaller block|With that the quene was wroth in hir maner, Thought she anon this ''towchith'' me right ner. {{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 560.}}}} 402 {{smaller block|The quarrel ''toucheth'' none but us alone. {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., iv. 1. 118.}}}} {{smaller block|These statutes ''touched'' high and low. {{right|''J. Gairdner'', Richard III., i.}}}} 26. To swindle; cheat; act dishonestly by: as, to ''touch'' one's mate. [Slang, Australia.]—'''To touch bottom''', {{smaller|to reach the lowest point, especially in price; have the least value.}}—'''To touch elbows.''' {{smaller|See ''elbow''.}}—'''To touch off.''' {{smaller|(''a'') To sketch hastily; finish by a few rapid touches or dashes.}} {{smaller block|I was upon this whispered, by one of the company who sat next me, that I should now see something ''touched off'' to a nicety. {{right|''Goldsmith'', Clubs.}}}} {{smaller|(''b'') To discharge, as a cannon.}}—'''To touch one on the raw.''' {{smaller|See ''raw''1.}}—'''To touch the gums''', {{smaller|in ''med.'', to cause incipient salivation by giving mercury.}}—'''To touch the wind''' {{smaller|(''naut.''), to keep the ship as near the wind as possible.}}—'''To touch up.''' {{smaller|(''a'') To repair or improve by slight touches or emendations; retouch: as, to ''touch up'' a picture. (''b'') To remind; jog the memory of. [Colloq.]}}—'''Touched bill of health.''' {{smaller|See ''bill of health'', under ''bill''3.}}—'''Touching the ears.''' {{smaller|See ''ear''1.}}—'''Touch me not.''' {{smaller|See ''touch-me-not''.}}—'''Touch pot, touch penny''', {{smaller|a proverbial phrase, signifying no credit given.}} {{smaller block|"We know the custom of such houses," continues he; "'tis ''touch pot, touch penny.''" {{right|''Graves'', Spiritual Quixote, iii. 2. (''Davies.'')}}}} II. ''intrans.'' 1. To be in contact; be in a state of junction, so that no appreciable space is between: as, two spheres ''touch'' only in one point. {{smaller block|Some side by side not ''touching'' walked,
As though of happy things they talked. {{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, III. 201.}}}} Specifically—2. To lay the hand or finger upon a person for the purpose of curing a disease, especially scrofula, or king's evil. {{smaller block|We were then shown Edward the Confessor's tomb; upon which Sir Roger acquainted us that he was the first that ''touched'' for the Evil. {{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 329.}}}} '''3'''†. To reach; extend. {{smaller block|The vois of people ''touchede'' to the hevene, So loude cryden they with mery stevene. {{right|''Chaucer'', Knight's Tale, l. 1703.}}}} '''4'''. To make a passing call, as a ship on a voyage: commonly with ''at'', rarely with ''on''. {{smaller block|And also Pole, which ys xxx myle from Parence, a good havyn, ffor many Shippys and galyes ''towche'' ther rather thanne ''at'' Parence. {{right|''Torkington'', Diarie of Eng. Travell, p. 16.}}}} {{smaller block|The next day we ''touched at'' Sidon. {{right|Acts xxvii. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|I made a little voyage round the lake, and ''touched on'' the several towns that lie on its coasts. {{right|''Addison'', Remarks on Italy (Works, ed. Bohn, I. 510).}}}} '''5'''. To mention or treat something slightly in discourse; refer cursorily or in passing: commonly with ''on'' or ''upon''. {{smaller block|Whenne the Sonne is Est in tho partyes, toward Paradys terrestre, it is thanne mydnyght in oure parties o this half, for the rowndenesse of the Erthe, of the whiche I have ''towched'' to zou before. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 303.}}}} {{smaller block|If the antiquaries have ''touched upon'' it, they have immediately quitted it. {{right|''Addison.''}}}} {{smaller block|The attitude and bearing of the law in this respect, ''on'' which I intend to ''touch'' in quite general terms. {{right|''Nineteenth Century'', XXVI. 841.}}}} {{smaller block|As soon as he hath ''touched on'' any science or study, he immediately seems to himself to have mastered it. {{right|''Bp. Atterbury'', Sermons, I. v.}}}} {{smaller block|Whenever she ''touch'd on'' me This brother had laugh'd her down. {{right|''Tennyson'', Maud, xix. 6.}}}} '''6'''. To bow or salute by touching the hat or cap. [Prov. Eng.]—'''7'''†. To rob. [Thieves' slang.]—'''8'''†. To stand the test. {{smaller block|As in London saith a Iuellere, Which brought from thence golde oore to us here, Whereof was fyned mettal good and clene, As they ''touch,'' no better could be seene. {{right|''Hakluyt's Voyages,'' I. 199.}}}} {{smaller block|And now you are brought to the test; ''touch'' right now, soldier, Now shew the manly pureness of thy mettle. {{right|''Fletcher,'' Loyal Subject, i. 5.}}}} 9†. To have or take effect; act. {{smaller block|Strong waters . . . will ''touch'' upon gold that will not ''touch'' upon silver. {{right|''Bacon.''}}}} 10. ''Naut.,'' of the sails of a square-rigged vessel, to be in such a position that their weather-leeches shake from the ship being steered so close to the wind.—'''To touch and go.''' {{smaller|(''a'') To touch lightly or briefly and pass on; dip in or stop for a moment here and there in course.}} {{smaller block|As the text doth rise, I will ''touch and go'' a little in every place. {{right|''Latimer,'' 1st Sermon bef. Edw. VI., 1549.}}}} {{smaller|(''b'') ''Naut.,'' to graze the bottom with the keel for a moment, as a vessel under sail, without lessening of the speed.—'''To touch on''' or '''upon.''' See def. 5.—'''Touch and trade papers.''' See ''paper.''}} '''touch''' (tuch), ''n.'' [< ME. ''touche;'' < ''touch, v.''] 1. That sense by which mechanical pressure upon the surface of the body (the skin, with the lips, the interior of the mouth, etc.) is perceived; sensibility to pressure, weight, and muscular resistance; the sense of feeling; taction. {{smaller|With this is sometimes reckoned sensibility to temperature. The sense of touch is most acute in those parts of the body that are freely movable, especially in the tips of the fingers. It is the most fundamental and least specialized or localized of the senses. See ''tactile corpuscles'', under ''corpuscle''.}} {{smaller block|Th' ear, Taste, ''touch'', and smell, pleased from thy table rise. {{right|''Shak.'', T. of A., i. 2. 132.}}}} {{smaller block|By ''touch'', hard, soft, rough, smooth, we do discern: By ''touch'', sweet pleasure and sharp pain we try. {{right|''Sir J. Davies'', Immortal. of Soul, xviii.}}}} {{smaller block|''Touch'' is . . . the sense by which mechanical force is appreciated, and it presents a strong resemblance to hearing, in which the sensation is excited by intermittent pressures on the auditory organ. {{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XXIII. 478.}}}} {{smaller block|All the senses are but modifications of ''touch''. {{right|''W. Wallace'', Epicureanism, p. 96.}}}} 2. Mental or moral feeling; moral perception or appreciation. {{smaller block|Can it be That men should live with such unfeeling souls, Without or ''touch'' or conscience of religion? {{right|''B. Jonson'', Case is Altered, v. 3.}}}} 3. Contact. {{smaller block|Never ''touch'' [was] well welcome to thy hand . . . Unless I . . . touch'd. {{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., ii. 2. 118.}}}} {{smaller block|But O, for the ''touch'' of a vanished hand, And the sound of a voice that is still! {{right|''Tennyson'', Break, break, break.}}}} 4. Figuratively, a close relation of mutual confidence, sympathy, interest, or the like; sympathy; accord or harmony in relation to common interests: as, to be out of ''touch'' with the times; to keep in ''touch'' with the people. {{smaller block|The European in Morocco feels that when he is in company with a Barbary Jew he is in ''touch'' with Europe. {{right|''The Academy'', June 1, 1889, p. 371.}}}} {{smaller block|We want, with our brethren of the working class, that which we have largely lost—the Church I fear not less than those who are outside of it—that expressive thing which we call ''touch''. {{right|''New Princeton Rev.'', II. 47.}}}} 5. Pressure, or application of pressure; impact; a slight stroke, tap, push, or the like: often used figuratively. {{smaller block|They [the Australians] pray to the Deuill, which hath conference with an Indian vnseene, from a peece of wood; and to him and all the rest many times by night he toucheth the face and breast with cold ''touches'', but they could neuer learne what he was. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 864.}}}} {{smaller block|A little ''touch'' of their adversary gives all that boisterous force the foil. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Alchemist, To the Reader.}}}} {{smaller block|Vineyards red with the ''touch'' of October. The grapes were gone, but the plants had a color of their own. {{right|''H. James, Jr.'', Little Tour, p. 173.}}}} 6. A slight or brief sound.—7. The impression conveyed to the mind by contact or pressure; effect on the sense of contact with something; feel: as, an object with a slimy ''touch''.—8. A jog; a hint; a reminder; a slight experience. {{smaller block|The king, your master, knows their disposition very well; a small ''touch'' will put him in mind of them. {{right|''Bacon''.}}}} {{smaller block|I . . . related unto you yt fearfull accidente, or rather judgmente, ye Lord pleased to lay on London Bridge, by fire and therin gave you a ''touch'' of my great loss. {{right|''Sherley'', quoted in Bradford's Plymouth Plantation, p. 308.}}}} 9. A stroke or dash as with a pen, pencil, or brush, literally or figuratively: as, a ''touch'' of bright color; also, any slight added effort or action, such as that expended on some completed work in order to give it finish. {{smaller block|What strained ''touches'' rhetoric can lend. {{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, lxxxii.}}}} {{smaller block|It tutors nature; artificial strife Lives in these ''touches'', livelier than life. {{right|''Shak.'', T. of A., i. 1. 38.}}}} {{smaller block|The old latticed windows, the stone porch, . . . the chimney stacks, were rich in crayon ''touches'', and sepia lights and shades.{{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Shirley, xi.}}}} 10. Figuratively, something resembling a light stroke or touch. (''a'') A tinge; a smack; a trace: as, a ''touch'' of irony. {{smaller block|No beast so fierce but knows some ''touch'' of pity.{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., i. 2. 71.}}}} {{smaller block|An insight into mechanics is desirable, with a ''touch'' of statistics.{{right|''Lamb'', Old and New Schoolmaster.}}}} {{smaller block|While the air has no ''touch'' of spring, Bird of promise! we hear thee sing.{{right|''Bryant'', Song Sparrow.}}}} (''b'') A shade; a trifle; a slight quantity or degree. {{smaller block|Madam, I have a ''touch'' of your condition, Which cannot brook the accent of reproof.{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iv. 4. 157.}}}} {{smaller block|Bell was a ''touch'' better educated than her husband.{{right|''Mrs. Gaskell'', Sylvia's Lovers, iv.}}}} (''c'') A taint; a blemish; a defect; an impairment. {{smaller block|How great a ''touch'' and wound that manner . . . is to his Reputation.{{right|''Sir R. Winwood'', Memorials, I. 448.}}}} {{smaller block|This ''touch'' in the brain of the British subject is as certainly owing to the reading newspapers as that of the Spanish worthy above-mentioned to the reading works of chivalry.{{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 178.}}}} (''d'') A slight attack or stroke; a twinge; a pang; a feeling: as, a ''touch'' of rheumatism. {{smaller block|Give me a rose, that I may press its thorns, and prove myself awake by the sharp ''touch'' of pain!{{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, x.}}}}
